stories.summary: US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin met in China for a historic trilateral summit, exchanging greetings and handshakes ahead of talks. The agenda remained unclear, with observers raising concerns about a possible carve-up of the global order into new spheres of influence. Trump described the summit as already a 'win' before the event. The meeting is being watched as a potential shift in the geometry of great-power politics.

stories.headline: COP31: India puts historical emissions burden back on the table
stories.summary: At COP31, India argued that developing countries should not be forced to carry the consequences of emissions historically generated by developed nations, placing climate equity and historical responsibility back at the centre of negotiations. It also sought a two-tier, country-driven Just Transition Mechanism. In parallel, ministers urged Türkiye and Australia to advance fossil fuel transition roadmaps, while Denmark and Spain announced new plans. Divisions persisted over energy policy, equity and financing, with developing countries pressing for greater financial support for a fair transition.
stories.whyItMatters: Directly tests the CBDR-RC principle, climate finance debates and India's negotiating position in UNFCCC COPs — key GS-III environment and GS-II global governance themes.

perspectives.take: Frames India's COP31 interventions as a reassertion of historical climate responsibility and a demand for a country-driven, two-tier Just Transition Mechanism, alongside ministerial pressure on Türkiye and Australia over fossil fuel transition roadmaps.

static.background: Common But Differentiated Responsibilities (CBDR-RC) is the core equity principle. Paris uses NDCs and a ratchet mechanism. The Loss & Damage fund was operationalised at COP28 (2023). India leads the International Solar Alliance (2015) and LiFE mission.

stories.headline: LeT commander Lateef Bhatt killed in Kulgam encounter
stories.summary: A Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT) commander identified as Lateef Bhatt was killed in an encounter with security forces in south Kashmir's Kulgam district, with the operation reported on 18 November. According to ThePrint, Bhatt had built a youth recruitment network in the Kulgam belt, and the forces tracked him through a trail that reportedly began with a dropped mobile phone and was corroborated by CCTV footage. The Tribune confirms the killing of the LeT commander in the Kulgam encounter, while Telegraph India highlights that an Army officer moved through heavy fire to evacuate 25 schoolgirls and two teachers before the commander was neutralised. Taken together, the accounts point to a small-unit, intelligence-led operation in which civilian evacuation and target neutralisation were interwoven, and to the continued salience of south Kashmir as an operational theatre for militant recruitment and counter-insurgency action.
stories.whyItMatters: Directly relevant to GS-III internal security — terrorism, role of non-state actors, and the intelligence-based counter-insurgency model in Jammu & Kashmir — and to GS-II on Centre–State security administration in a Union Territory. The case also illustrates how recruitment networks, rather than only attacks, have become the priority target of the security grid.

perspectives.take: Frames the killing as the outcome of patient technical and human intelligence work — a recruitment-network builder tracked down, with a dropped phone and CCTV trail as the investigative spine (national, security-establishment-friendly framing).
Reports the event factually and tersely as a confirmed counter-insurgency success, foregrounding the identity of the militant and the location (north-India regional daily, restrained tone).

Humanises the operation by leading with the officer who risked fire to evacuate 25 girls and two teachers, framing it as a rescue-before-elimination story (Kolkata-based national daily, narrative/valour angle).

static.topic: Counter-insurgency in Jammu & Kashmir
static.syllabusNode: Internal Security — Role of external state and non-state actors in creating internal security challenges; security forces and agencies
static.whatIsIt: The three-tier security grid in J&K — Army (including Rashtriya Rifles), Central Armed Police Forces such as the CRPF, and the J&K Police with its Special Operations Group — conducts intelligence-based 'targeted operations' against militant outfits such as Lashkar-e-Taiba, Jaish-e-Mohammed and Hizbul Mujahideen.
static.background: Militancy in the Kashmir Valley escalated from the late 1980s; Pakistan-based outfits and cross-border infiltration shaped the 1990s. After the 2001 Parliament attack and the 2008 Mumbai attacks, India's response combined diplomatic pressure, UAPA/NIA legal architecture and a revamped intelligence grid. J&K was reorganised into a Union Territory with effect from 31 October 2019 under the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019, following the abrogation of Article 370. Since then, security policy has centred on targeting militant command and recruitment structures while managing law-and-order and political transition.
static.geography: Kulgam is a district in south Kashmir within the Kashmir Valley; south Kashmir districts (Kulgam, Shopian, Pulwama, Anantnag, Awantipora belt) have accounted for a large share of recent encounters and militant recruitment.
static.socioEconomic: Recruitment narratives in the Valley are commonly analysed in terms of local grievances — youth unemployment, alienation, internet and social-media radicalisation, and the aftermath of security operations. Counter-insurgency success is therefore assessed not only by militant casualties but by whether recruitment pipelines and local support bases shrink.
static.whyInNews: A Lashkar-e-Taiba commander identified as Lateef Bhatt, described as having built a youth recruitment network in the Kulgam area, was killed in an encounter in Kulgam district.
static.wayForward: Shift from kinetic-only metrics to a combined approach: intelligence-led precision operations with strict adherence to human-rights safeguards, community policing, rehabilitation of surrendered youth, verification of custody and encounter procedures, and addressing the governance and employment deficits that recruitment networks exploit.
prelimsPointers: Lashkar-e-Taiba is a Pakistan-based militant outfit founded in 1990 and led by Hafiz Muhammad Saeed; it is banned in India under the UAPA and is listed by the UN Security Council's 1267 sanctions committee.
Kulgam is a south Kashmir district; south Kashmir has been a persistent focus of counter-insurgency operations.
static.mainsAngle: Intelligence-led targeted operations have reduced militant command structures in J&K, yet recruitment persists. Critically examine whether kinetic dominance alone can deliver durable internal security in the Valley.

static.topic: Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act and the NIA framework
static.syllabusNode: Internal Security — Terrorism; laws and institutions for countering organised crime and terrorism
static.whatIsIt: The UAPA, 1967 is India's principal anti-terror statute; the National Investigation Agency (NIA), created in 2008, is the central counter-terror investigation agency with powers to take over cases across States.
static.background: The UAPA was originally enacted in 1967 to deal with unlawful associations and was substantially strengthened by amendments in 2004, 2008 and 2019. The 2019 amendment allowed the Centre to designate individuals (not only organisations) as terrorists. The NIA Act, 2008 followed the 26/11 Mumbai attacks to enable central investigation of terror offences, with special courts and a defined schedule of offences.
static.whyInNews: Encounters with proscribed outfits such as LeT sit within the broader legal architecture of proscription under the UAPA and central counter-terror investigation by the NIA.
static.wayForward: Balance robust counter-terror powers with procedural safeguards — timely chargesheeting, judicial oversight of detention, and transparent review of designations — so that security effectiveness is not undermined by due-process challenges.
prelimsPointers: The UAPA was enacted in 1967; the 2019 amendment enabled designation of individuals as terrorists.
The NIA was created under the NIA Act, 2008, in the aftermath of the 26/11 Mumbai attacks.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how India's anti-terror legal framework has evolved since 1967, and evaluate the balance it strikes between security imperatives and civil liberties.

static.topic: UN Security Council counter-terrorism sanctions regime (1267 Committee)
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Important international institutions; global governance and multilateral reform
static.whatIsIt: The UN Security Council's 1267 sanctions committee administers the consolidated list of individuals and entities associated with terrorism, imposing asset freezes, travel bans and arms embargoes. The UNSC is a principal organ of the UN with five permanent veto-wielding members (P5) and ten elected members serving two-year terms.
static.background: Resolution 1267, adopted in 1999, established the Al-Qaida/Taliban sanctions committee; the regime was subsequently strengthened through later resolutions. Because listing decisions are taken by consensus among the 15 UNSC members, listings can be blocked by any member, which is why India has long pressed for the listing of Pakistan-based individuals and entities. India is a founding UN member and among the largest troop contributors to UN peacekeeping.
static.whyInNews: The neutralisation of an LeT commander in Kulgam re-focuses attention on Pakistan-based proscribed outfits and on the international listing and sanctions architecture that India uses to press its counter-terror case globally.
static.wayForward: India continues to push for comprehensive reform of the UNSC, including expansion of permanent and non-permanent seats (the G4 effort with Brazil, Germany and Japan), while also pursuing financial and travel sanctions on terror financiers through the 1267 regime and the Financial Action Task Force process.
prelimsPointers: The UNSC has 15 members — 5 permanent (China, France, Russia, UK, USA) with veto power and 10 elected for two-year terms.
UN sanctions against listed terror entities are administered by the 1267 Committee; listing requires consensus among UNSC members.
static.mainsAngle: India's counter-terror diplomacy relies on global sanctions regimes that are hostage to UNSC politics. Examine, in this light, the case for Security Council reform.

prelims: Lashkar-e-Taiba is a Pakistan-based militant organisation founded in 1990 under Hafiz Muhammad Saeed; it is proscribed in India under the UAPA and listed by the UN Security Council's 1267 sanctions committee.
Kulgam is a district in south Kashmir, a region that has consistently recorded a high share of encounters and militant recruitment in the Valley.
Intelligence-led 'targeted operations' in J&K typically involve the Army/Rashtriya Rifles, the CRPF and the J&K Police's Special Operations Group acting on technical and human intelligence inputs.
The UAPA (1967, amended in 2004, 2008 and 2019) and the NIA Act, 2008 form the legal-institutional core of India's counter-terror framework.
stories.mainsQuestion: Intelligence-led targeted operations have become the dominant template of counter-insurgency in Jammu & Kashmir. Examine how far this approach has degraded militant command structures, and evaluate whether it can, by itself, address the recruitment and radicalisation dynamics that sustain militancy in the Valley.

stories.headline: Bangladesh deploys paramilitary as unrest grows over Hasina's return
stories.summary: Bangladesh has called in paramilitary forces to contain spreading unrest linked to the political question of former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina's return. Police reports cited by the media record dozens of crude bomb blasts and incidents of vehicles being torched across at least 28 districts over the past ten days, with several police personnel and civilians injured. The disturbances indicate that the country's post-transition political contestation is now spilling onto the streets well beyond the capital. The deployment of paramilitary units signals that the civil administration and police alone are seen as insufficient to hold order. For India, the turmoil in a bordering neighbour raises immediate questions of border security, connectivity projects and the political handling of Hasina's presence on Indian soil.
stories.whyItMatters: Instability in Bangladesh directly affects India's eastern border security, trade and connectivity, and tests the Neighbourhood First approach — a recurring GS-II theme on India and its neighbourhood.

perspectives.take: Frames the story through on-the-ground law-and-order data — blast and arson counts across 28 districts and casualties among police and civilians — emphasising the scale of internal disorder.

static.topic: India–Bangladesh Relations
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — India and its Neighbourhood
static.whatIsIt: A comprehensive bilateral relationship spanning a shared land border, trade and transit, water sharing, security and border management, connectivity and people-to-people ties. Bangladesh is central to India's eastern neighbourhood and to the Act East and Neighbourhood First frameworks.
static.background: India supported Bangladesh's liberation struggle in 1971 and recognised the new state that year. The two sides signed a Treaty of Friendship in 1972, the Land Boundary Agreement (1974, operationalised in 2015 with enclave exchange), the Ganga Waters Treaty in 1996, and an Extradition Treaty in 2013. Relations deepened through the 2010s with connectivity, power and transit cooperation. Bangladesh underwent a major political transition in 2024 following the ouster of Sheikh Hasina's government, after which an interim arrangement took charge and Sheikh Hasina's presence in India became a politically charged issue in Bangladesh.
static.geography: Bangladesh lies almost entirely enclosed by India on the west, north and east, with the Bay of Bengal to the south; it shares land borders with only India and Myanmar. The India–Bangladesh border runs through West Bengal, Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram.
static.socioEconomic: Bangladesh is among India's largest trading partners in South Asia, with Indian exports of cotton, machinery, electricity and food items, and Bangladeshi exports of readymade garments, jute and fish. Cross-border movement of people, labour and informal trade is substantial, and Indian connectivity projects — rail links, ports of call and transit arrangements — depend on political stability in Dhaka.
static.whyInNews: Bangladesh has deployed paramilitary forces amid unrest over the question of Sheikh Hasina's return, with police recording crude bomb blasts and vehicle torching in at least 28 districts over ten days.
static.wayForward: India is likely to continue engaging whichever government holds office in Dhaka, while safeguarding connectivity and energy projects, managing border and refugee-related spillovers, and handling the politically sensitive question of Hasina's stay through legal and diplomatic channels rather than public posturing.
prelimsPointers: India's longest land border is with Bangladesh (roughly 4,096 km).
Bangladesh shares land borders with only two countries — India and Myanmar.
static.mainsAngle: Political instability in a bordering neighbour compels India to balance security, connectivity and humanitarian concerns; evaluate how India's Bangladesh policy should adapt to rapid political change.

static.topic: Neighbourhood First and India's Strategic Autonomy
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — India and the World; Foreign Policy
static.whatIsIt: India's foreign policy orientation that combines strategic autonomy and multi-alignment with a deliberate prioritisation of South Asian neighbours under the Neighbourhood First outlook, alongside maritime outreach under SAGAR and the Act East Policy.
static.background: Rooted in the Non-Aligned Movement (1961) and the Panchsheel principles (1954), India's approach was reshaped by the 1991 liberalisation and the 1998 nuclear tests. Neighbourhood First has been articulated as a governing principle since 2014, with SAGAR (2015) extending it to the Indian Ocean, and simultaneous engagement through the Quad, BRICS, SCO, G20 and IBSA.
static.geography: South Asia's geography of shared rivers, porous borders and narrow land corridors makes India's ties with Bangladesh, Nepal, Bhutan, Sri Lanka, Maldives and Myanmar structurally interdependent.
static.socioEconomic: Regional stability underpins Indian trade routes to the northeast, transit rights, hydropower and port access, and the livelihoods of border communities; disruption in any one neighbour raises costs across the region.
static.whyInNews: The unrest in Bangladesh is a live test of India's neighbourhood policy, given India's deep economic and security stakes and the political sensitivity surrounding Sheikh Hasina's presence in India.
static.wayForward: Sustained quiet diplomacy, protection of ongoing connectivity and energy projects, and consistent engagement with whichever dispensation holds power in Dhaka would preserve India's long-term interests while avoiding entanglement in domestic political contests.
prelimsPointers: Neighbourhood First has been a stated governing principle of Indian foreign policy since 2014; SAGAR was articulated in 2015.
BBIN (Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Nepal) is a sub-regional connectivity framework launched in 2015.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how political turbulence in South Asian states tests India's Neighbourhood First policy, and suggest how India can protect its strategic and economic interests without appearing to intervene in domestic politics.

prelims: Bangladesh has deployed paramilitary forces after police recorded dozens of crude bomb blasts and vehicle-torching incidents across at least 28 districts in ten days.
Bangladesh shares land borders with only two countries — India and Myanmar — and India's border with it is the longest India shares with any neighbour.

stories.mainsQuestion: Political instability in Bangladesh carries direct consequences for India's eastern border, connectivity and regional diplomacy. Discuss the challenges such turbulence poses to India's Neighbourhood First policy and suggest a calibrated response.

stories.headline: ICJ to rule on Myanmar's alleged genocide of Rohingya
stories.summary: The International Court of Justice is set to deliver a verdict in the case alleging genocide against Myanmar's Rohingya minority. The case, brought by The Gambia under the Genocide Convention, accuses Myanmar of mass killings, rape and forced displacement. If the court finds Myanmar responsible, it would be the first time an international court has held a state guilty of genocide. The ruling is expected to test both the reach of international law and the enforcement capacity of the UN system.
stories.whyItMatters: Tests the ICJ's role in enforcing the Genocide Convention and the limits of international legal accountability for state crimes; useful for GS-II international law and global governance.

perspectives.take: Frames the verdict as historic because no state has ever been found guilty of genocide by an international court, highlighting the gravity and precedent-setting nature.

static.topic: International Court of Justice & Genocide Convention
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — International Law
static.whatIsIt: The ICJ is the principal judicial organ of the UN, established in 1945 by the UN Charter and ICJ Statute. It settles legal disputes between states and gives advisory opinions. The Genocide Convention (1948) makes genocide a crime under international law and obliges states to prevent and punish it.
static.background: The Gambia filed a case against Myanmar at the ICJ in 2019 alleging genocide against the Rohingya. In 2020, the ICJ ordered provisional measures to prevent genocide and preserve evidence. In 2022, the ICJ rejected Myanmar's preliminary objections and affirmed its jurisdiction. A final verdict on the merits is now awaited.
static.geography: The ICJ sits in the Peace Palace, The Hague, Netherlands.
static.whyInNews: The ICJ is set to deliver a verdict that could mark the first time an international court finds a state guilty of genocide.
static.wayForward: Enforcement of ICJ judgments depends on state compliance and UNSC action; strengthening the Genocide Convention's implementation and early-warning mechanisms is essential.
prelimsPointers: ICJ is the principal judicial organ of the UN; it is distinct from the International Criminal Court (ICC).
ICJ judgments are binding on parties, but the court has no independent enforcement power; non-compliance may be referred to the UNSC.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss the effectiveness of the ICJ and the Genocide Convention in delivering accountability for mass atrocities, and suggest reforms to overcome enforcement deficits.

stories.headline: Board of Peace warns Gaza ceasefire could collapse as Israel, Hamas stall
stories.summary: President Donald Trump's Board of Peace has warned that the Gaza ceasefire could unravel unless Israel and Hamas recommit to the pledges they made during negotiations. The truce has halted major fighting, but the wider plan — Hamas disarmament, Israeli troop withdrawal and reconstruction — has effectively stalled since soon after it took effect. By publicly faulting both parties, the Board has signalled that the mechanism meant to shepherd the deal is not delivering. Reporting on the $18 billion pledged to the Board adds a funding-accountability dimension to the impasse. Taken together, the accounts describe a ceasefire that is holding militarily but failing politically and financially.
stories.whyItMatters: Directly relevant to GS-II questions on West Asia, the durability of externally brokered peace mechanisms, and India's stakes in regional stability — energy security, the Gulf diaspora and connectivity projects.

static.topic: Gaza ceasefire and the Board of Peace
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Effect of policies and politics of developed and developing countries on India's interests; bilateral, regional and global groupings and agreements
static.whatIsIt: A ceasefire arrangement in Gaza overseen by a 'Board of Peace' constituted by US President Donald Trump, intended to move from a halt in fighting to Hamas disarmament, Israeli troop withdrawal and reconstruction.
static.background: The Gaza conflict has been punctuated by repeated, short-lived truces brokered by Qatar, Egypt and the United States. The current arrangement emerged from negotiations involving Israel and Hamas and was placed under a US-convened Board of Peace. Its wider implementation has stalled since soon after it took effect, and the Board has now publicly faulted both parties.
static.geography: The Gaza Strip is a narrow Mediterranean coastal territory bordering Israel and Egypt and is among the most densely populated areas in the world; the Rafah crossing with Egypt and Israeli-controlled crossings are its principal entry points.
static.socioEconomic: Prolonged conflict and blockade have left the population heavily aid-dependent, with large-scale displacement, destroyed housing and infrastructure, and reconstruction costs far exceeding the funds pledged so far.
static.whyInNews: The Board of Peace warned that the ceasefire could collapse if Israel and Hamas do not recommit to their pledges, while reporting questioned what has happened to the $18 billion pledged to the Board.
static.wayForward: Sequenced implementation with verifiable milestones, a credible monitoring mechanism, unblocked humanitarian access, and transparent, traceable disbursement of pledged reconstruction funds.
prelimsPointers: The Gaza Strip borders Israel and Egypt; the Rafah crossing is its main link to Egypt.
UNRWA, the UN agency for Palestinian refugees, was created by the UN General Assembly in 1949.
The Oslo Accords (1993) between Israel and the PLO created the Palestinian Authority and divided the West Bank into Areas A, B and C.
static.mainsAngle: Examine why externally brokered ceasefire mechanisms in West Asia stall at the implementation stage, and what institutional design could make them durable.

static.topic: India's stakes in West Asia and the Palestinian question
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — India and its neighbourhood-relations; bilateral, regional and global groupings and agreements involving India and/or affecting India's interests
static.whatIsIt: India's West Asia policy balances de-hyphenated ties with Israel, historic support for the Palestinian cause, and deep energy, trade and diaspora links with the Gulf states.
static.background: India recognised Israel in 1950, but full diplomatic relations began only in 1992. India has consistently supported a two-state solution and has voted at the UN in line with that position, while simultaneously expanding defence, agriculture and technology cooperation with Israel and connectivity and energy ties with Gulf partners.
static.geography: West Asia spans the Arabian Peninsula, the Levant and Iran; the Strait of Hormuz and Bab-el-Mandeb are chokepoints critical to India's energy imports and trade routes.
static.socioEconomic: Gulf states host a large Indian diaspora and are a major source of remittances; the region supplies a substantial share of India's crude oil and LPG, making regional stability directly relevant to Indian inflation and the current account.
static.whyInNews: Renewed uncertainty over the Gaza ceasefire affects regional stability, humanitarian access and the wider normalisation and connectivity agenda in which India has an interest.
static.wayForward: Continue principled support for a two-state solution and international humanitarian law, sustain humanitarian assistance, and protect energy, trade and diaspora interests through balanced engagement with all regional partners.
prelimsPointers: India established full diplomatic relations with Israel in 1992.
The India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC) was announced at the 2023 G20 Summit in New Delhi.
The Strait of Hormuz connects the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and is a key global oil chokepoint.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how instability in West Asia tests India's balancing act between its strategic partnership with Israel and its historical and economic ties with the Arab world.

stories.headline: India imposes 162.5% levy on bulk Scotch amid UK trade pact standoff

The levy applies to bulk Scotch imports, raising costs for importers and potentially consumers. The development underscores how tariff policy can become a bargaining chip in bilateral trade negotiations.

stories.headline: IAF wants Astra missile, own data link on 114 Rafale jets
stories.summary: The Indian Air Force has tied its requirement for 114 multirole fighter aircraft to two non-negotiable conditions: the freedom to integrate its own weapons and the ability to operate the fleet on an Indian data link. The Astra beyond-visual-range air-to-air missile, developed by DRDO, is the immediate test case, with the service wanting to fit it on the Rafale without waiting on the original equipment manufacturer for integration clearances. Equally, the IAF wants the aircraft to communicate over a national network rather than a vendor-controlled one, so that the fleet plugs into India's own command-and-control architecture. Together, the demands signal a deliberate push against vendor lock-in in a large, long-tenure procurement, where control over software, weapons and networks determines how independently a platform can be used.
stories.whyItMatters: It captures the central tension in Indian defence acquisition — buying capable foreign platforms while retaining sovereign control over weapons, software and networks. This is directly examinable under GS-III security, self-reliance and defence procurement policy.

perspectives.take: Frames the 114-jet programme as a test of the IAF's insistence on operational sovereignty — own weapons and own network rather than vendor-locked systems; an exclusive, defence-establishment-sourced report that foregrounds the service's negotiating position.

static.topic: MRFA: Procurement of 114 Multirole Fighter Aircraft
static.syllabusNode: Security — Defence procurement, Defence Acquisition Procedure and the Strategic Partnership model
static.whatIsIt: A long-pending Indian Air Force programme to acquire 114 multirole combat aircraft through a competitive global tender with substantial indigenous manufacture, intended to arrest the decline in fighter squadron strength.
static.background: The IAF's sanctioned strength is 42 fighter squadrons, but actual holdings have stayed well below that for years. An earlier tender for 126 medium multirole combat aircraft was withdrawn, and was followed by a government-to-government purchase of 36 Rafale aircraft from France in 2016. The 114-aircraft requirement was subsequently revived under the Defence Acquisition Procedure, which lays down categories such as Buy (Indian-IDDM), Buy (Indian), Buy and Make, and Buy (Global), with indigenisation weighted heavily.
static.socioEconomic: Large offset and Make-in-India manufacturing obligations are expected to draw in domestic aerospace suppliers and MSMEs, with employment and technology-transfer implications for the Indian defence industrial base.
static.whyInNews: The IAF has made weapons-integration autonomy and an indigenous data link conditions of the 114-aircraft requirement, with the Rafale as the platform under discussion.
static.wayForward: Treat source-code, weapons-integration and data-link access as non-negotiable contractual clauses rather than post-contract negotiations; build DRDO and public-sector integration capacity in parallel; sequence the programme alongside Tejas Mk-2 and AMCA so that capability gaps do not widen during negotiations.
prelimsPointers: The IAF's sanctioned strength is 42 fighter squadrons; actual strength has remained well below it.
DAP 2020 governs Indian defence procurement and places 'Buy (Indian-IDDM)' at the top of the priority order.
The 2016 Rafale purchase was a government-to-government deal with France for 36 aircraft.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how India's fighter aircraft procurement strategy reconciles urgent capability gaps, indigenisation targets and the demand for operational sovereignty.

static.topic: Astra Beyond-Visual-Range Air-to-Air Missile
static.syllabusNode: Security — Indigenisation of defence technology; missiles and aerospace systems
static.whatIsIt: Astra is India's indigenous beyond-visual-range air-to-air missile, developed by DRDO and produced by Bharat Dynamics Limited, designed to be integrated across multiple IAF fighter platforms.
static.background: Developed by DRDO over roughly two decades with flight trials conducted from the Su-30MKI, Astra has been integrated on the Su-30MKI and the Tejas. Successive variants — Mk-I, Mk-II and planned follow-ons — progressively extend range and improve seeker and propulsion capability, including work on a solid fuel ducted ramjet concept for longer ranges.
static.socioEconomic: Domestic missile production supports Bharat Dynamics Limited and a chain of private suppliers, and reduces foreign exchange outflow on imported beyond-visual-range missiles.
static.whyInNews: The IAF wants Astra fitted on the Rafale fleet, making it the immediate test of the service's demand for weapons-integration freedom on imported platforms.
static.wayForward: Complete integration and certification trials on imported platforms, expand production capacity to meet wartime stockholding norms, and mature Astra Mk-II and ramjet-based variants to close the range gap with foreign equivalents.
prelimsPointers: Astra is India's indigenous beyond-visual-range air-to-air missile, developed by DRDO and produced by Bharat Dynamics Limited.
It has been integrated on the Su-30MKI and the Tejas.
Astra variants (Mk-I, Mk-II and planned follow-ons) progressively increase range and seeker capability.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how indigenous missile programmes such as Astra reduce dependence on foreign suppliers and strengthen the IAF's combat capability.

static.topic: Data Links and Network-Centric Warfare
static.syllabusNode: Security — Defence communication, network-centric warfare and cybersecurity
static.whatIsIt: A data link is a secure digital channel that lets aircraft, ground radars and command centres exchange target and situational data in real time; an indigenous data link keeps that network under national control rather than a foreign manufacturer's.
static.background: The IAF operates the Integrated Air Command and Control System (IACCS) as its principal air-defence network, fusing radar and sensor feeds. India has been working on indigenous communication systems, including software-defined radio, to reduce reliance on foreign equipment for secure military networking. Control over data links has become a standard point of contention in foreign platform purchases because it determines who can modify, certify and secure the network.
static.socioEconomic: Domestic electronics, communications and cryptography firms gain from indigenous networking programmes, while dependence on foreign OEMs for secure network equipment carries strategic and cost risks.
static.whyInNews: The IAF has insisted that the 114-aircraft fleet operate on an Indian data link rather than a vendor-controlled network.
static.wayForward: Standardise an indigenous data link across fighter, airborne early warning and ground segments; certify it for interoperability with existing IACCS architecture; and strengthen domestic cryptographic certification so that network security is not outsourced.
keyTerms: Integrated Air Command and Control System (IACCS)
prelimsPointers: Data links enable real-time sharing of sensor and targeting data among aircraft, radars and command centres.
The IAF's Integrated Air Command and Control System (IACCS) is its principal air-defence network.
static.mainsAngle: Analyse why control over communication networks and weapons integration is central to military operational sovereignty in an era of network-centric warfare.

stories.headline: COP31 endgame: finance gap, fossil roadmaps and mountain risk
stories.summary: As COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, entered its final week, developing countries were still pressing for the climate finance they were promised, with equity and delivery — not new declarations — dominating the negotiations. Commentators argued that the gap is no longer one of ambition on paper but of speed, resources and cooperation, warning that postponing action shifts a climate bill onto the next generation. In parallel, mountain fragility was thrust into the spotlight: a proposal to add an agenda item on the impacts of rising temperatures on high mountain ranges was reportedly rejected, yet the catastrophic downstream consequences of glacier and snowpack loss continued to shape discussions. On the domestic side, attention turned to how India can mobilise resources for its own climate action, signalling that the finance debate is now as much internal as multilateral.
stories.whyItMatters: COP31 outcomes feed directly into GS-III questions on climate finance, CBDR-RC and the Global Stocktake, and into GS-II debates on the credibility of multilateral environmental governance. Mountain-specific risk also links climate change to disaster management and Himalayan ecology.

static.topic: Climate Change Regime & India's Commitments
static.syllabusNode: Environment — Climate Change
static.whatIsIt: The UNFCCC (1992) is the parent treaty; the Kyoto Protocol (1997) and Paris Agreement (2015) operationalise it. India targets net-zero by 2070 and 50% installed non-fossil capacity by 2030.
static.background: Common But Differentiated Responsibilities (CBDR-RC) is the core equity principle. Paris uses NDCs and a ratchet mechanism. The Loss & Damage fund was operationalised at COP28 (2023). India leads the International Solar Alliance (2015) and the LiFE mission.
static.geography: Global regime with differentiated obligations; India's commitments are domestic-economy wide, with Himalayan and coastal vulnerability as key physical drivers.
static.socioEconomic: Climate finance determines the pace of transition in developing economies; unmet finance shifts costs to public budgets, households and future generations.
static.whyInNews: COP31 in Antalya entered its final week with developing countries still seeking promised finance, and with India-focused work on domestic resource mobilisation for climate action.
static.wayForward: Close the finance gap through predictable, grant-based and concessional flows; strengthen adaptation and Loss & Damage delivery; align domestic resource mobilisation with NDC targets.
prelimsPointers: India's updated NDC: cut emissions intensity of GDP by 45% from 2005 levels by 2030.
Paris Agreement goal: keep warming well below 2°C, ideally 1.5°C.
static.mainsAngle: Climate finance and technology transfer gaps; examine equity in the Global Stocktake and just transition.

static.topic: United Nations & Multilateral Reform
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Global Governance
static.whatIsIt: The UN (1945) has six principal organs; the Security Council has five permanent veto-wielding members (P5) and ten elected members. India has long sought permanent UNSC membership.
static.background: India is a founding UN member and one of the largest troop contributors to peacekeeping. The G4 (India, Brazil, Germany, Japan) campaigns for expansion. Intergovernmental Negotiations (IGN) on Security Council reform remain inconclusive.
static.socioEconomic: Representation deficits in multilateral bodies shape whether developing countries' finance and technology demands are treated as entitlements rather than concessions.
static.whyInNews: COP31 negotiations under the UNFCCC framework renewed scrutiny of whether multilateral processes deliver equitably for developing countries.
static.wayForward: Push for reform of multilateral institutions alongside climate negotiations so that decision-making reflects current economic and demographic realities.
prelimsPointers: UNSC has 15 members: 5 permanent + 10 elected for 2-year terms.
ICJ is in The Hague; UN HQ is in New York.
static.mainsAngle: India's claim rests on representativeness, its population and contributions; assess obstacles such as veto politics and the Ezulwini Consensus.

static.topic: Mountain Ecosystems and Climate Risk
static.syllabusNode: Environment — Mountain Ecosystems & Disaster Management
static.whatIsIt: High mountain ranges — including the Hindu Kush Himalaya, often called the Third Pole — are climate-sensitive systems where glacier retreat, changing snowfall patterns and glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF) risk threaten downstream water, energy and food security.
static.background: The National Mission for Sustaining the Himalayan Ecosystem (NMSHE) is one of the missions under the National Action Plan on Climate Change (NAPCC, 2008). India has experienced damaging GLOF-linked disasters, including in Chamoli (2021) and Sikkim (2023).
static.geography: Hindu Kush Himalaya, Andes, Alps and Rockies; the Himalayan arc feeds major river systems on which South Asian populations depend.
static.socioEconomic: Downstream agriculture, hydropower, tourism and mountain livelihoods are exposed; adaptation costs fall heavily on resource-constrained hill states and communities.
static.whyInNews: A proposal to include an agenda item at COP31 on the impacts of rising temperatures on high mountain ranges was reportedly rejected, but mountain fragility remained a prominent theme in the talks.
static.wayForward: Mainstream mountain-specific adaptation into climate negotiations and national planning; invest in glacier monitoring, early warning systems and GLOF risk reduction.
prelimsPointers: NMSHE is one of the missions under the National Action Plan on Climate Change (2008).
The Hindu Kush Himalaya is described as the Third Pole, holding the largest ice reserves outside the polar regions.
static.mainsAngle: Examine why mountain regions need dedicated adaptation finance and institutional attention within the UNFCCC process.

prelims: COP31 was held in Antalya, Türkiye, with the final week dominated by climate finance demands from developing countries.
The UNFCCC (1992) is the parent treaty; the Kyoto Protocol (1997) and Paris Agreement (2015) operationalise it.
The Loss & Damage fund was operationalised at COP28 (2023).
India's climate targets: net-zero by 2070, 50% installed non-fossil capacity by 2030, and a 45% cut in emissions intensity of GDP from 2005 levels by 2030.
stories.mainsQuestion: Climate negotiations increasingly suffer from a delivery gap rather than an ambition gap. In this context, examine the obstacles to fulfilling climate finance commitments and suggest how equity principles such as CBDR-RC can be operationalised, including for vulnerable mountain regions.

stories.headline: Java flaw, spy-network outage, AI attack tool: 2026's mounting cyber failures
stories.summary: A newly disclosed security flaw in Java — a programming language embedded in a vast range of enterprise and consumer software — has triggered urgent security advisories worldwide, with users urged to patch and harden their systems. Separately, a US spy agency's classified network reportedly suffered an outage during maintenance, an episode that underlines the fragility of even the most protected systems. These incidents sit within a year marked by repeated cyberattacks and service outages at major technology providers including Microsoft, AWS and Google. Reporting also highlights ARTEX, an AI-based penetration-testing tool being repurposed to power attacks, indicating how AI is lowering the cost and raising the speed of cyber offensives.

static.topic: Cyber Security and Critical Infrastructure Resilience

static.whatIsIt: Cyber security within India's internal-security framework covers protection of critical information infrastructure, incident response and cyber-crime investigation, coordinated through the MHA, CERT-In, NCIIPC and agencies such as the NIA.
static.background: Left-wing extremism peaked in the 'Red Corridor' and the SAMADHAN doctrine guides counter-LWE operations, while AFSPA applies to notified disturbed areas. Integrated Command and Control Centres and NATGRID were built to strengthen security-related information sharing, and CERT-In functions as the national nodal agency for cyber-incident response.
static.geography: Not geography-specific; cyber threats are cross-border and affect networked infrastructure globally.
static.socioEconomic: Deep digital dependence of banking, health, power and transport raises the economic cost of outages, with small firms and individuals bearing disproportionate losses.
static.whyInNews: A new Java security flaw triggered urgent advisories worldwide, a US spy agency's classified network reportedly suffered an outage during maintenance, and 2026 has seen repeated cyberattacks and outages at major cloud providers.
static.wayForward: Institutionalise patch management and vulnerability-disclosure norms, strengthen sectoral CERTs, enforce mandatory incident reporting, conduct cyber drills for critical infrastructure, and build cyber-forensics workforce capacity.

static.topic: Digital Public Infrastructure and Data Protection
static.syllabusNode: Governance — e-Governance & Data Governance
static.whatIsIt: India's Digital Public Infrastructure — Aadhaar, UPI and DigiLocker — is a layered, interoperable stack, while the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 governs the processing of personal data.
static.background: Aadhaar (UIDAI, 2009) is the world's largest biometric ID system; UPI (NPCI, 2016) processes billions of monthly transactions; the DPDP Act introduced a Data Protection Board and consent-based processing.
static.socioEconomic: DPI lowers transaction costs and widens financial inclusion, but concentrates sensitive data, making breaches and outages systemically consequential.
static.whyInNews: Repeated outages and cyberattacks on globally used software and cloud platforms highlight the exposure of large digital ecosystems, including India's DPI, to supply-chain and vulnerability risks.
static.wayForward: Strengthen breach-notification and audit regimes under the DPDP framework, build redundancy into DPI rails, and invest in indigenous security testing and assurance.
prelimsPointers: NPCI operates UPI, RuPay, IMPS and NACH.
The DPDP Act provides for consent, data-principal rights and significant data fiduciaries.

static.topic: Primary Markets and IPO Regulation in India
static.syllabusNode: Economy — Capital Markets; SEBI and securities regulation
static.whatIsIt: An IPO is the first sale of shares by a company to the public, moving it from private to listed status. In India, public issues are regulated by SEBI under the SEBI Act, 1992 and the SEBI (Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, alongside the Companies Act, 2013. Pricing typically happens through book-building within a disclosed price band, with separate allotment categories for retail, institutional and non-institutional investors, and mandatory disclosure through a red herring prospectus.
static.background: SEBI was constituted in 1988 and given statutory powers through the SEBI Act, 1992, in the wake of securities-market irregularities of the early 1990s. The BSE, established in 1875, is among the world's oldest exchanges, while the NSE was set up in the 1990s and introduced electronic screen-based trading. Dematerialised settlement and depositories followed in the mid-1990s, and India moved to a T+1 settlement cycle in 2023. IPO activity in India has historically been cyclical, with sharp waves of retail participation.
static.geography: India — primary market activity is concentrated in Mumbai as the financial capital, with exchanges BSE and NSE based there.
static.socioEconomic: IPOs channel household savings into equity and provide growth capital to firms, but heavy retail participation in over-subscribed issues raises investor-protection concerns about pricing and disclosure quality.

static.wayForward: Strengthen disclosure standards and investor education, deepen domestic institutional participation, and review listing norms periodically so that capital formation keeps pace with the pipeline of technology firms seeking public markets.

stories.headline: Supreme Court issues contempt notice to advocate over remarks against CJI
stories.summary: The Supreme Court has initiated contempt proceedings against an advocate over remarks directed at the Chief Justice of India, which the Court treated as 'unworthy' and derogatory. static.topic: Supreme Court, High Courts and Judicial Review

static.whatIsIt: The Supreme Court (Article 124) is the apex court and guardian of the Constitution; High Courts (Article 214) sit at the state level. Judicial review is the power to test legislative and executive action against the Constitution, exercised through writ jurisdiction under Articles 32 and 226.
static.background: The collegium system evolved through the Three Judges Cases (1981, 1993, 1998). Kesavananda Bharati (1973) established the basic-structure doctrine. PILs expanded access to justice from the late 1970s. Articles 32 and 226 provide writ jurisdiction, while Articles 129 and 215 make the Supreme Court and High Courts courts of record with the power to punish for contempt.
static.whyInNews: The Supreme Court has issued a contempt notice to an advocate over remarks against the Chief Justice of India, bringing the Court's protective jurisdiction over its own dignity into focus.
static.wayForward: Contempt proceedings should remain a last-resort response reserved for conduct that genuinely obstructs or scandalises the administration of justice, with reasoned, proportionate orders so that institutional authority is preserved without chilling fair criticism.

static.topic: Contempt of Court and the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Judiciary: powers of constitutional courts
static.whatIsIt: Contempt of court is broadly of two kinds — civil contempt (wilful disobedience of a court order) and criminal contempt (acts that scandalise the court, prejudice judicial proceedings, or obstruct the administration of justice). The power flows from Articles 129 and 215 and is codified and regulated by the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971.
static.background: Articles 129 and 215 declare the Supreme Court and High Courts courts of record with the power to punish for contempt. The Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 defined and limited the power, distinguishing civil from criminal contempt. The Contempt of Courts (Amendment) Act, 2006 inserted Section 13(b), allowing truth as a defence if it is bona fide and in the public interest. Courts have historically invoked contempt suo motu in cases involving scurrilous attacks on judges.
static.whyInNews: A contempt notice to an advocate over remarks against the CJI raises the question of where legitimate criticism of judges ends and scandalising the court begins.
static.wayForward: Courts may prefer reasoned disapproval or procedural safeguards over harsh punishment in borderline speech cases, while the legislature could consider clearer statutory guidance on scandalising the court, so that contempt does not become a tool to suppress criticism.

stories.headline: Pew projects Muslims may outnumber Christians globally by 2035
stories.summary: A Pew Research Center study projects that Muslims could become the world's largest religious group by around 2035, overtaking Christians, with higher fertility rates cited as the principal driver. By 2070, Muslim populations are also forecast to grow substantially, while demographic shifts are expected to alter religious majorities in countries such as the United States and Canada. These figures are projections built on assumptions about fertility, mortality, migration and religious switching rather than observed outcomes, and are therefore conditional scenarios rather than predictions.
stories.whyItMatters: Population projections connect fertility differentials to social composition, making them relevant to GS-I questions on society, diversity and population, and to debates on demographic transition and its policy consequences. The item also tests whether candidates understand how demographers construct projections and the limits of such forecasts.

stories.headline: India, Canada eye defence pact during Modi's December visit
stories.summary: India and Canada are working towards a defence cooperation pact to be firmed up around Prime Minister Narendra Modi's planned visit to Canada in December, according to reporting by The Hindu. India's High Commissioner to Ottawa framed the engagement as a deliberate reset, arguing that the two countries share extensive mutual interests and cannot allow fringe issues to derail the relationship. The reported move follows a period of diplomatic strain in bilateral ties and signals a step-by-step normalisation through high-level political contact. If concluded, a defence pact would add a security pillar to a relationship currently dominated by trade, energy, education and diaspora links. The report reflects India's official position and does not carry a corresponding Canadian government articulation.
stories.whyItMatters: A defence pact with a G7, NATO and Five Eyes member tests India's multi-alignment in practice, showing how strategic autonomy is operationalised when a partner is both a Western security actor and a source of recent political friction. It is a live case study for GS-II questions on bilateral relations, diaspora politics and the balance between principled positions and pragmatic engagement.

perspectives.take: Frames the story through the Indian official lens — the High Commissioner's argument that shared interests outweigh 'fringe issues' — presenting the defence pact as a pragmatic reset ahead of a December visit; carries no Canadian counter-framing.

articles.title: India, Canada eye defence pact during Modi visit in December
articles.snippet: India’s High Commissioner to Ottawa says both countries cannot afford to let fringe issues derail their extensive mutual interests

static.topic: India–Canada Relations
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Bilateral Relations (India and North America)
static.whatIsIt: A wide-ranging bilateral relationship covering political dialogue, defence and security, trade and investment, energy, education, agriculture and one of the world's largest Indian-origin diasporas. Both countries are Commonwealth members and G20 economies.
static.background: Canada supplied the CIRUS research reactor, and cooperation was frozen after India's 1974 nuclear test. Ties were rebuilt after India's 1998 tests, with Canada supporting India's 2008 NSG waiver and the two signing a civil nuclear cooperation agreement that came into force in 2013. Negotiations for a Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) were launched in 2022 but were paused amid the 2023 diplomatic rupture triggered by Canadian allegations over the killing of a Sikh separatist leader on Canadian soil, which India rejected. Engagement resumed gradually through 2025 with renewed high-level contacts.
static.geography: Canada is a North American, Arctic and Atlantic-Pacific state; its 2022 Indo-Pacific Strategy explicitly covers India. The Indian-origin population is concentrated in Ontario and British Columbia.
static.socioEconomic: Canada hosts a large Indian-origin diaspora and is a major destination for Indian students. Bilateral trade spans goods and services, while Canada supplies uranium, potash and pulses to India, and Canadian pension funds are significant investors in Indian infrastructure.
static.whyInNews: A defence cooperation pact is being eyed around Prime Minister Modi's planned December visit, as reported by The Hindu.
static.wayForward: Institutionalise defence and trade dialogues so that they survive political shocks, conclude the pending CEPA, and route diaspora and extremism concerns through legal and consular channels rather than public recrimination.
prelimsPointers: Canada is not a member of the Quad; it is a member of the G7, NATO and the Five Eyes intelligence alliance.
Canada released its Indo-Pacific Strategy in 2022, which identifies India as a key partner.
India–Canada CEPA negotiations were launched in 2022 and subsequently paused.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how domestic political sensitivities in a partner country can constrain India's bilateral engagement, and suggest institutional mechanisms to insulate core economic and security cooperation from such shocks.

static.topic: India's Foreign Policy and Strategic Autonomy
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — India and the World
static.whatIsIt: India's foreign policy combines strategic autonomy, multi-alignment, and the Neighbourhood First and Act East outlooks, engaging simultaneously across the Quad, BRICS, SCO, G20 and IBSA.
static.background: Rooted in NAM (1961) and Panchsheel (1954). Post-1991 liberalisation and the 1998 nuclear tests reshaped ties with the US. The Indo-Pacific concept and the Quad (with the US, Japan and Australia) gained salience after 2017.
static.socioEconomic: Economic diplomacy — trade agreements, energy sourcing, technology partnerships and diaspora engagement — is a core instrument of this strategy.
static.whyInNews: The reported India–Canada defence pact is a test case of multi-alignment: deepening security cooperation with a Western partner while maintaining independent positions on issues of domestic political sensitivity.
static.wayForward: Sustain issue-based engagement with all major partners, keep defence and economic tracks de-linked from political disputes, and articulate India's positions clearly to avoid misperception.
prelimsPointers: India assumed the G20 presidency in 2022–23; the African Union was admitted as a permanent G20 member in 2023.
India and Pakistan joined the SCO in 2017.
static.mainsAngle: Balancing ties with the West, Russia and the Global South; assess India's role as a 'Voice of the Global South' and bridging power.

static.topic: Defence Diplomacy and Defence Cooperation Agreements
static.syllabusNode: Security — Defence Cooperation and Defence Diplomacy
static.whatIsIt: Defence diplomacy uses framework agreements — memoranda of understanding, logistics support arrangements and industrial cooperation pacts — to structure military-to-military engagement, exercises, information sharing and co-development.
static.background: India has progressively signed foundational defence arrangements with key partners, including the Logistics Exchange Memorandum of Agreement (LEMOA, 2016), COMCASA (2018) and BECA (2020) with the United States, the Acquisition and Cross-Servicing Agreement with Japan (2020) and a mutual logistics support arrangement with Australia (2020).
static.socioEconomic: Defence industrial cooperation creates scope for joint ventures, technology transfer and export market access, feeding into India's push for self-reliance in defence manufacturing.
static.whyInNews: A defence pact with Canada is reported to be under discussion ahead of a December visit.
static.wayForward: Prioritise niche, deliverable cooperation — maritime domain awareness, cyber, peacekeeping training and defence industrial co-development — over symbolic agreements.
prelimsPointers: LEMOA was signed with the United States in 2016; COMCASA in 2018 and BECA in 2020.
India signed an Acquisition and Cross-Servicing Agreement with Japan in 2020 and a mutual logistics support arrangement with Australia in 2020.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how logistics and defence framework agreements enhance India's operational reach, and evaluate the strategic risks of deepening defence ties with Western partners.

prelims: Canada is not a member of the Quad; it belongs to the G7, NATO and the Five Eyes intelligence alliance.
India and Canada are both Commonwealth members and G20 economies; their CEPA negotiations, launched in 2022, were later paused.
Canada released its Indo-Pacific Strategy in 2022, which identifies India as a key partner.
Canada is a significant supplier of uranium, potash and pulses to India, and hosts a large Indian-origin diaspora.
stories.mainsQuestion: The reported India–Canada defence pact ahead of a December visit suggests a pragmatic reset. Examine how India's doctrine of strategic autonomy shapes such resets, and discuss the opportunities and constraints in India–Canada defence and economic cooperation.

stories.headline: India needs a comprehensive space security doctrine, not weaponisation
stories.summary: An op-ed argues that India lacks a comprehensive doctrine on space security even as its civilian and strategic dependence on satellites deepens. The author's central framing is that India's objective should not be to convert outer space into another arena of conflict, but to ensure that any disruption in space does not translate into vulnerability on Earth. This shifts the emphasis from offensive counterspace capabilities towards resilience, deterrence by denial and norm-building. The argument draws on the wider debate over space debris, dual-use technologies and the fragile legal architecture governing orbital activity.
stories.whyItMatters: Space is now critical infrastructure for communication, navigation, remote sensing and missile warning, making space security a cross-cutting GS-III (Science & Technology, Security) and GS-II (Global Governance, Disarmament) theme for both Prelims and Mains.

perspectives.take: Frames space security as a doctrine gap rather than a capability gap, urging India to prioritise preventing disruption and terrestrial vulnerability over militarising orbit — a restraint-oriented, Indian-editorial line.

articles.title: India needs a comprehensive doctrine on space security
articles.snippet: India’s objective should not be to turn outer space into another arena of conflict, but to ensure that disruption in space does not translate into vulnerability on Earth

static.topic: India's Space Programme (ISRO)
static.syllabusNode: Science & Technology — Space
static.whatIsIt: ISRO, established in 1969 and functioning under the Department of Space, runs India's space programme covering communication, remote sensing, navigation (NavIC) and planetary exploration. IN-SPACe (2020) and NSIL were created to enable and commercialise private participation.
static.background: Aryabhata (1975) was India's first satellite. Mangalyaan (2013) reached Mars orbit on the first attempt, and Chandrayaan-3 soft-landed near the lunar south pole in 2023. Gaganyaan is India's first crewed mission, while Aditya-L1 is a solar observatory mission.
static.socioEconomic: Satellite services underpin telecommunications, weather forecasting, agriculture advisory, disaster warning and financial timing systems, so disruption in orbit has direct economic and social costs on the ground.
static.whyInNews: The op-ed argues that India's expanding space assets need a matching doctrine on space security rather than an ad hoc response to threats.
static.wayForward: Institutionalise a publicly articulated space security doctrine that integrates civil, commercial and defence space actors, strengthens ISRO's dual-use governance, and aligns capability-building with resilience and debris mitigation.
prelimsPointers: PSLV is India's workhorse launcher, while GSLV Mk-III (LVM3) can carry heavier geosynchronous payloads.
India is a founder participant in the Outer Space Treaty framework, with UN COPUOS as the principal forum for space law.
NavIC is India's regional satellite navigation system.
static.mainsAngle: Commercialisation of space, space debris mitigation and India's role in shaping space governance.

static.topic: Outer Space Treaty and Space Security Governance
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Global Governance and Disarmament
static.whatIsIt: The 1967 Outer Space Treaty is the foundational instrument of international space law; it prohibits placing weapons of mass destruction in orbit, reserves celestial bodies for peaceful purposes, and holds states liable for objects they launch. UN COPUOS oversees its implementation, while PAROS discussions on preventing an arms race in outer space have long been stalled at the Conference on Disarmament.
static.background: Negotiated during the Cold War and opened for signature in 1967, the treaty reflects a period of bipolar restraint. Later instruments addressed registration, liability and astronaut rescue. India has consistently advocated peaceful uses of outer space and opposed the weaponisation of orbit, while itself demonstrating limited ASAT capability through Mission Shakti in 2019.
static.whyInNews: The op-ed's call for an Indian space security doctrine sits within the wider debate over whether existing treaty architecture is adequate for contemporary counterspace threats such as jamming, cyber intrusions and debris-generating tests.
static.wayForward: India can push for transparency and confidence-building measures in COPUOS, strengthen space situational awareness sharing, and evolve domestic norms on debris mitigation and dual-use technology export.
prelimsPointers: The Outer Space Treaty prohibits weapons of mass destruction in orbit but does not ban conventional or directed-energy counterspace systems.
India conducted Mission Shakti, an anti-satellite missile test, in March 2019, becoming the fourth country to demonstrate such a capability.
PAROS is discussed at the Conference on Disarmament, not at COPUOS.
static.mainsAngle: Evaluate whether existing international space law is sufficient to prevent an arms race in outer space, and assess India's stake in norm-building versus capability development.

prelims: India's space programme is administered by the Department of Space, with ISRO as the executing agency; IN-SPACe and NSIL handle promotion and commercialisation of private space activity.
The 1967 Outer Space Treaty bans weapons of mass destruction in orbit but does not prohibit other counterspace capabilities such as jamming or cyber operations.
India demonstrated a limited anti-satellite capability through Mission Shakti in 2019, becoming the fourth country to do so after the United States, Russia and China.
NavIC is India's indigenous regional satellite navigation system, used for positioning and timing services over India and the surrounding region.
stories.mainsQuestion: India's growing dependence on space-based assets makes space security both an economic and a strategic imperative. Discuss the contours of a comprehensive national space security doctrine, and examine whether India should prioritise norm-building in multilateral forums over the development of counterspace capabilities.

stories.headline: US prosecutors allege second murder target in Pannun assassination plot
stories.summary: US prosecutors have alleged that Vikash Yadav and Nikhil Gupta, already accused in the reported plot to kill Sikhs for Justice leader Gurpatwant Singh Pannun on American soil, also planned a second killing during the same period. The claim is an allegation contained in US legal proceedings and has not been established in an Indian court; New Delhi has previously said it constituted a high-level enquiry committee to examine the matter. The case sits at the intersection of counter-terrorism, extradition and diplomatic practice between two partners that otherwise cooperate closely on defence, technology and the Indo-Pacific. Indian commentary has largely reported the prosecutorial claim factually, while Pakistani commentary has used it to argue that the episode reflects a wider pattern of Indian covert action, including in Jammu and Kashmir. The story therefore matters less for its unproven specifics than for what it reveals about how allegations of transnational violence are litigated in the public domain.
stories.whyItMatters: It is a live test of India–US bilateral trust and of how international law, extradition treaties and sovereignty claims interact when one state's courts allege state-linked violence by another's personnel. It also feeds directly into GS-II international relations and GS-III internal security questions on extremism, diaspora politics and accountability.

perspectives.take: Reports the US prosecutors' allegation as a factual development in an ongoing criminal case, foregrounding the named individuals and the legal process rather than drawing wider political conclusions.

Frames the indictment as evidence of a broader Indian 'playbook' of covert operations and narrative control, drawing a parallel with encounters in Indian-administered Jammu and Kashmir — a Pakistani outlet with a clear adversarial regional lens.
