static.topic: India–US Relations: Strategic Partnership and Diplomatic Frictions
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Bilateral Relations (India and USA)
static.whatIsIt: The India–US relationship is a broad strategic partnership covering defence, trade, technology, energy, counter-terrorism and the Indo-Pacific, but it is periodically tested by legal and consular disputes, including extradition requests and allegations involving Indian nationals or former officials.
static.background: The 1997 India–US Extradition Treaty (in force from 1999) is the legal channel for such requests. Ties deepened after the 2005 civil nuclear agreement, the 2008 IAEA safeguards agreement and NSG waiver, the 2016 designation of India as a Major Defence Partner, the 2+2 Ministerial Dialogue, the Quad and the 2023 initiative on Critical and Emerging Technology (iCET).
static.socioEconomic: A large Indian-American diaspora, deep services and technology linkages, and growing defence and energy trade give both sides strong incentives to contain legal disputes rather than let them escalate.
static.whyInNews: US prosecutors have alleged that two individuals already accused in the reported Pannun murder plot also planned a second killing, keeping a sensitive legal case in the bilateral spotlight.
static.wayForward: India can continue to cooperate with the US judicial process through established mutual legal assistance and extradition channels while insisting that allegations against individuals are not treated as findings against the state.
prelimsPointers: The India–US Extradition Treaty was signed in 1997 and entered into force in 1999.
India was designated a Major Defence Partner of the United States in 2016.
The India–US 2+2 Ministerial Dialogue involves the foreign and defence ministers of both countries.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how legal and consular disputes test a strategic partnership, and assess the adequacy of existing bilateral mechanisms for resolving them.

static.topic: Transnational Repression, Extradition and International Law
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — International Law, Sovereignty and Effect of Policies of Developed Countries on India's Interests
static.whatIsIt: Transnational repression refers to a state's attempts to reach dissidents, activists or suspects beyond its own borders through surveillance, intimidation, abduction or violence. It raises questions of sovereignty, jurisdiction and the limits of lawful counter-terrorism cooperation.
static.background: The UN Charter (Article 2(4)) prohibits the threat or use of force against the territorial integrity of another state, and Article 2(7) bars intervention in domestic jurisdiction. The Vienna Convention on Consular Relations, 1963, governs notification and access when a national is detained abroad, while extradition and mutual legal assistance treaties provide the lawful route for securing suspects. In this case, Nikhil Gupta was arrested in the Czech Republic in 2023 and extradited to the United States in 2024, and India constituted a high-level enquiry committee in November 2023 to examine the allegations.
static.whyInNews: Fresh US prosecutorial allegations of a second intended killing have revived debate on how states may lawfully pursue suspects abroad and how such claims are adjudicated.
static.wayForward: Strengthen domestic investigative and oversight mechanisms, use treaty-based channels rather than unilateral action, and press for clear evidentiary standards when foreign courts examine allegations involving state personnel.
prelimsPointers: Article 2(4) of the UN Charter prohibits the threat or use of force against another state's territorial integrity and political independence.
The Vienna Convention on Consular Relations, 1963, deals with consular notification and access for detained foreign nationals.
Extradition is normally governed by bilateral treaties or multilateral conventions rather than by customary law alone.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss the tension between counter-terrorism imperatives and respect for the sovereignty of other states, with reference to recent allegations of transnational operations.

static.topic: Khalistan Extremism and Diaspora Security
static.syllabusNode: Internal Security — Extremism, Role of Non-State Actors and Security Challenges
static.whatIsIt: A section of the overseas Sikh diaspora has backed the demand for a separate 'Khalistan', with Sikhs for Justice (SFJ) running a so-called referendum campaign. India treats these outfits as unlawful and as a threat to internal security and communal harmony.
static.background: The Khalistan movement peaked in Punjab in the 1980s and declined after the 1985 Rajiv–Longowal Accord and sustained policing. SFJ was founded in 2007 by Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, a US citizen. India declared SFJ an unlawful association under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act in 2019 and designated Pannun an individual terrorist under the same law in 2020. The 2023 killing of Hardeep Singh Nijjar in Canada and the subsequent US indictment brought the issue into wider international focus.
static.geography: Punjab shares a land border with Pakistan; the diaspora is concentrated in Canada, the United States, the United Kingdom and Australia.
static.socioEconomic: Diaspora remittances and Punjab's agrarian and industrial economy are sensitive to prolonged unrest and to any deterioration in overseas community relations.
static.whyInNews: The reported US indictment naming a second intended target is part of the same cluster of allegations linked to the Pannun case.
static.wayForward: Combine firm legal action against designated outfits with sustained engagement of moderate diaspora opinion, and pursue evidence-based cooperation with host countries rather than allowing the narrative to be set by adversarial framing.
prelimsPointers: SFJ was declared an unlawful association under the UAPA in 2019, and Gurpatwant Singh Pannun was designated an individual terrorist under the UAPA in 2020.
The National Investigation Agency was created under the NIA Act, 2008, after the 2008 Mumbai attacks.
The Rajiv–Longowal Accord of 1985 was an attempt to restore normalcy in Punjab.
static.mainsAngle: Evaluate India's legal and diplomatic toolkit for countering overseas extremist campaigns while protecting the interests of the wider diaspora.

prelims: The India–US Extradition Treaty was signed in 1997 and came into force in 1999.
Sikhs for Justice was declared an unlawful association under the UAPA in 2019; Gurpatwant Singh Pannun was designated an individual terrorist under the UAPA in 2020.
Nikhil Gupta was arrested in the Czech Republic in 2023 and extradited to the United States in 2024 in connection with the alleged plot.
India constituted a high-level enquiry committee in November 2023 to examine the allegations relating to the case.
stories.mainsQuestion: Allegations of transnational assassination plots have complicated India's relations with key Western partners. Examine the legal, diplomatic and internal security challenges such allegations pose, and suggest a way forward that upholds both national security and respect for international law.

stories.headline: Ayushman Bharat widens government hospital packages from 23 to 112
stories.summary: The Tribune reports that the Ayushman Bharat scheme is set to expand the basket of treatment packages available at government hospitals from 23 to 112. The change widens the range of procedures that can be availed at public facilities under the scheme's insurance-linked benefit package, rather than being routed largely to private empanelled hospitals. The reported expansion sits within Ayushman Bharat's existing two-pillar design — the PM-JAY health-insurance arm and the network of Health and Wellness Centres — and is aimed at strengthening the public-hospital leg of the delivery chain. Details of rates, rollout timelines and the implementing authority's notification are not specified in the report.
stories.whyItMatters: Directly relevant to GS-II welfare and social-justice questions on health financing, and to prelims facts on PM-JAY's architecture, coverage and implementing institutions. It also feeds the debate on whether insurance-led expansion can substitute for strengthening public health infrastructure.

perspectives.take: Frames the development as a scheme-design expansion — more government-hospital packages under Ayushman Bharat — with emphasis on widening public-facility treatment options; a mainstream national daily, no strong ideological slant, but light on cost and implementation detail.

articles.title: Ayushman Bharat scheme to expand government hospital packages from 23 to 112
articles.snippet: Ayushman Bharat scheme to expand government hospital packages from 23 to 112 The Tribune

static.topic: Ayushman Bharat (PM-JAY) and India's welfare architecture
static.syllabusNode: Social Justice — Welfare & Rights (Health)
static.whatIsIt: Ayushman Bharat is India's flagship health-assurance programme, built on two pillars: the Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (PM-JAY), which provides health insurance for secondary and tertiary hospitalisation, and Health and Wellness Centres (now Ayushman Arogya Mandirs) for comprehensive primary care. It sits within India's wider welfare model that blends rights-based laws (MGNREGA 2005, RTE 2009, NFSA 2013) with DBT-enabled delivery over the JAM (Jan Dhan–Aadhaar–Mobile) backbone.
static.background: Ayushman Bharat was announced in the 2018 Union Budget and launched in 2018, with PM-JAY as its insurance arm and Health and Wellness Centres as its primary-care arm. PM-JAY provides cover of ₹5 lakh per family per year for secondary and tertiary care hospitalisation, with no cap on family size or age, and is implemented by the National Health Authority (NHA) with Centre–State cost sharing. The scheme's benefit package has been revised periodically to add procedures and rationalise rates.
static.socioEconomic: Health shocks are a leading cause of catastrophic out-of-pocket spending and debt among low-income households; insurance-led schemes aim to reduce this, but exclusion errors, low awareness and weak empanelment in some regions limit uptake.
static.whyInNews: The Tribune reports that government hospital packages under Ayushman Bharat are being expanded from 23 to 112, widening the procedures available at public facilities.
static.wayForward: Pair package expansion with public-hospital capacity — specialist manpower, diagnostics, drugs and referral systems — and with transparent, regularly updated empanelment and grievance data so that the expansion translates into actual treatment, not just entitlements on paper.
keyTerms: Health and Wellness Centres / Ayushman Arogya Mandir
prelimsPointers: Ayushman Bharat (2018) has two pillars: PM-JAY for health insurance and Health and Wellness Centres for primary care.
PM-JAY gives ₹5 lakh per family per year for secondary and tertiary hospitalisation, with no cap on family size or age.
The National Health Authority is the apex body implementing PM-JAY; funding is shared between the Centre and States.
static.mainsAngle: Examine whether insurance-based welfare schemes such as PM-JAY can deliver universal health coverage without parallel investment in public health infrastructure and human resources.

static.topic: Health Benefit Packages and public hospital capacity
static.syllabusNode: Government Policies & Interventions — Health; Infrastructure: Social Sector
static.whatIsIt: A Health Benefit Package (HBP) is the notified list of procedures, along with their rates and conditions, that are reimbursed under PM-JAY. Expanding the number of packages available specifically at government hospitals changes where beneficiaries can seek treatment and how public facilities are paid for it.
static.background: PM-JAY began with a defined set of surgical and medical packages, and the package list and rates have been revised periodically, including a comprehensive revision in 2022. Public hospitals have historically been a smaller share of empanelled providers than private ones, so package design for government facilities is a lever for shifting care towards the public system.
static.socioEconomic: Out-of-pocket expenditure remains a substantial share of India's total health spending, and public hospitals are the fallback for households that cannot afford private care; expanding their package coverage can reduce referral-driven costs but requires them to have the specialists and equipment to deliver the procedures.
static.whyInNews: The reported jump from 23 to 112 government hospital packages is a change in the benefit-package design for public facilities under Ayushman Bharat.
static.wayForward: Link package expansion to time-bound upgrading of district hospitals and medical colleges, outcome-based payment, and monitoring of denial rates and referral patterns so that public facilities are not merely listed but actually able to deliver.
prelimsPointers: PM-JAY covers secondary and tertiary care hospitalisation, not outpatient primary care, which is handled by Ayushman Arogya Mandirs.
The Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission, launched in 2021, seeks to build digital health infrastructure including health IDs and registries.
The National Health Policy, 2017 set a long-term target for government health expenditure as a share of GDP.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how the design of health benefit packages shapes the balance between public and private provision of secondary and tertiary care in India.

prelims: Ayushman Bharat, launched in 2018, rests on two pillars: PM-JAY (health insurance) and Health and Wellness Centres, now called Ayushman Arogya Mandirs.
PM-JAY provides ₹5 lakh per family per year for secondary and tertiary care hospitalisation, with no restriction on family size or age.
The National Health Authority is the apex implementing body for PM-JAY, with joint Centre–State funding.
The scheme's Health Benefit Package — the notified list of covered procedures and rates — is revised periodically.
stories.mainsQuestion: The expansion of hospital packages under Ayushman Bharat widens entitlements at government facilities. Critically examine whether insurance-led expansion alone can improve access to secondary and tertiary care, and suggest the institutional and financial reforms needed to make public hospitals the preferred first point of care.

stories.headline: Census 2027 drops 200-plus entries from 'other' religion list, adopts predictive text
stories.summary: The Census 2027 portal has replaced the drop-down menu for the 'Other' religion option with a predictive-text field, and in the process has dropped more than 200 entries that had appeared in the earlier list. The change follows reporting that at least 287 entries — including ISKCON, Gorak Nath, Sanatan, Vedic Dharm and Ramdev — had briefly appeared in the drop-down and were then withdrawn. The 'Other' option is a write-in category used when a respondent's faith is not covered by the listed major religions, and such responses are subsequently classified by the census authorities. The revision indicates that the enumeration machinery is still finalising how self-declared religious identities will be captured and coded in the 2027 exercise.
stories.whyItMatters: The census is the foundational data set for delimitation, welfare targeting and minority policy, so how religious identity is recorded and classified directly affects representation and public debate. For the exam, it links constitutional secularism and self-declaration with the administrative design of India's first digital census.

perspectives.take: Frames the issue as one of transparency and process in the census portal, following up its own earlier report on the 287-entry drop-down and highlighting the shift to predictive text and the removal of over 200 entries; a mainstream national daily, it emphasises official clarification over communal framing.

articles.title: Census 2027: ‘Other’ religions list made predictive text, over 200 entries from earlier list dropped
articles.snippet: This comes days after The Hindu reported that at least 287 entries such as ISKCON, Gorak Nath, Sanatan, Vedic Dharm, Ramdev etc. had been listed in a drop-down menu for “Other” religions on the portal and then removed

static.topic: Census 2027
static.syllabusNode: Population and associated issues — Census as a source of demographic data
static.whatIsIt: Census 2027 will be India's 16th decennial census and the first to be conducted digitally, with self-enumeration and a mobile application, and the first to include caste enumeration alongside the existing schedule.
static.background: Census-taking in India began in 1872 on a non-synchronous basis and became synchronous from 1881 under Lord Ripon. Since independence it has been conducted under the Census Act, 1948, with the Office of the Registrar General and Census Commissioner functioning under the Ministry of Home Affairs. The 2021 census was postponed because of the COVID-19 pandemic; the government subsequently announced that the census would be held in 2027, with house-listing operations preceding enumeration and a reference date of March 1, 2027 (October 1, 2026 for snow-bound areas).
static.geography: Conducted across all States and Union Territories; snow-bound regions use an earlier reference date than the rest of the country.
static.socioEconomic: Census figures underpin delimitation of constituencies, reservation-related policy, welfare scheme targeting, fiscal devolution and nearly all official demographic and socio-economic statistics.
static.whyInNews: The 'Other' religion option on the Census 2027 portal, which had briefly displayed 287 entries, has been converted into a predictive-text field, with over 200 of those entries dropped.
static.wayForward: Publish the final religion code list and the coding protocol for write-in responses well before enumeration begins, so that the treatment of self-declared identities is transparent and open to scrutiny.
prelimsPointers: Census 2027 will be the 16th census of India and the first to be conducted digitally.
Reference date: March 1, 2027; October 1, 2026 for snow-bound areas.
Census is a Union List subject (Entry 69) and is conducted under the Census Act, 1948.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how the digitalisation of the census — self-enumeration, portal design and automated coding — affects data quality, privacy and the inclusivity of the enumeration process.

static.topic: Enumeration of religion and constitutional secularism
static.syllabusNode: Indian Constitution — secularism; Fundamental Rights (Articles 25–28)
static.whatIsIt: The census records religion on the basis of self-declaration. The schedule provides a fixed set of major religion codes along with an 'Other' option in which a respondent may write in a faith not listed; published data also carry an 'Other Religions and Persuasions' (ORP) category.
static.background: Religion has been canvassed in Indian censuses since 1872, and religion-wise data have been published through the post-independence censuses. The Constitution does not permit the state to compel disclosure of religion in a manner that violates Articles 25–28, and census responses are voluntary in practice, with confidentiality protected under the Census Act.
static.socioEconomic: Religion-wise census data feed directly into debates on minority welfare schemes, reservation policy, and the political salience of religious demography.
static.whyInNews: The handling of the 'Other' religion field on the Census 2027 portal has revived questions about how the state classifies religious self-identification.
static.wayForward: Adopt a published, consultative and stable classification protocol so that write-in religious identities are neither arbitrarily excluded nor inconsistently grouped.
prelimsPointers: Religion is recorded in the census through self-declaration, not official verification.
Published census tables carry an 'Other Religions and Persuasions' category for faiths outside the major religions.
Articles 25–28 guarantee freedom of conscience and the right to profess, practise and propagate religion.

static.topic: Census administration: Census Act, 1948 and the RGI
static.syllabusNode: Government policies and interventions; statutory and executive bodies
static.whatIsIt: The Census Act, 1948 empowers the Central Government to conduct the census, and the Office of the Registrar General and Census Commissioner of India, under the Ministry of Home Affairs, is the nodal authority for its planning and execution.
static.background: The Census Act was enacted in 1948 and the first census under it was conducted in 1951; the Census Rules, 1990, govern operational details. The Act provides for confidentiality of individual returns and penalises refusal or false returns.
static.socioEconomic: The legal framework makes the census a centralised exercise, which is why portal design, schedules and code lists are decided by the Union rather than by States.
static.whyInNews: Changes to the religion field on the Census 2027 portal are administrative decisions taken within this statutory framework.
static.wayForward: Use the pre-enumeration period for wider stakeholder consultation on schedule design, and place the final schedules and code lists in the public domain.
prelimsPointers: The census is conducted under the Census Act, 1948, with rules framed in 1990.
'Census' is Entry 69 of the Union List, making it a subject on which only Parliament can legislate.
The Registrar General and Census Commissioner of India functions under the Ministry of Home Affairs.
static.mainsAngle: Critically evaluate the centralised statutory framework of census administration in the light of demands for greater transparency and stakeholder consultation.

prelims: Census 2027 will be India's 16th census and the first digital census, with a reference date of March 1, 2027 (October 1, 2026 for snow-bound areas).
The census is conducted under the Census Act, 1948, by the Office of the Registrar General and Census Commissioner under the Ministry of Home Affairs; 'Census' is Entry 69 of the Union List.
Religion is recorded through self-declaration; the schedule lists major religions with an 'Other' write-in option, and published data carry an 'Other Religions and Persuasions' category.
The Census 2027 portal has replaced the 'Other' religion drop-down with a predictive-text field, dropping over 200 of the 287 entries that had earlier appeared.
stories.mainsQuestion: The census is both a statistical exercise and a statement about how the Indian state recognises its people. In this light, examine the implications of the recent changes to the 'Other' religion field on the Census 2027 portal for transparency, secularism and data quality.

onThisDay.title: Operation Uranus launched at Stalingrad
onThisDay.description: During World War II, Soviet forces under General Georgy Zhukov launched Operation Uranus, a massive counteroffensive that encircled Axis troops at Stalingrad. It marked the turning point of the Battle of Stalingrad and the wider Eastern Front in favour of the USSR.
onThisDay.upscLink: World History: WWII and Soviet counteroffensive; turning point on Eastern Front.

onThisDay.title: Reagan and Gorbachev meet in Geneva
onThisDay.description: US President Ronald Reagan and Soviet General Secretary Mikhail Gorbachev met for the first time in Geneva during the Cold War. The summit helped initiate a thaw in superpower relations and later arms-control negotiations.
onThisDay.upscLink: Cold War diplomacy, US-Soviet relations, and arms control.

onThisDay.title: Anwar Sadat addresses the Knesset
onThisDay.description: Egyptian President Anwar Sadat addressed the Israeli Knesset in Jerusalem, calling for peace between Egypt and Israel. His visit paved the way for the Camp David Accords and the Egypt-Israel peace treaty.
onThisDay.upscLink: West Asia peace process; Camp David Accords and Egypt-Israel relations.

onThisDay.title: Apollo 12 lands on the Moon
onThisDay.description: Apollo 12 astronauts Pete Conrad and Alan Bean landed at Oceanus Procellarum and became the third and fourth humans to walk on the Moon. The mission was the second crewed lunar landing in NASA's Apollo programme.
onThisDay.upscLink: Space exploration; Apollo programme and the US-Soviet space race.

onThisDay.title: China launches Shenzhou 1
onThisDay.description: China launched its first Shenzhou spacecraft, an uncrewed test flight that marked a major step in its human spaceflight programme. It laid the foundation for China's later crewed missions and space station ambitions.
onThisDay.upscLink: Science and Technology: China's space programme; global space race.
